newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Maskhadov Chechnya win seen good for oil industry.
newsitem.headline: Maskhadov Chechnya win seen good for oil industry.

text.p: Aslan Maskhadov's victory in Chechen presidential elections on Sunday, followed by soothing words that oil would be able to move safely across his country, were welcomed by analysts and energy executives on Friday.
They said the new president of independence-minded Chechnya had a realistic chance of stabilising the war-torn region, removing a major political risk to Caspian Sea oil projects.
"His victory is very important, because Maskhadov will follow rational policies," said Sergei Markov, political analyst at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace think-tank.

Russia's Deputy Fuel and Energy Minister Anatoly Shalatov told Itar-Tass news agency on Friday Maskhadov had guaranteed the safety of crude oil flowing through Chechnya and that repairs to a pipeline through the republic would soon begin.
A pipeline linking huge oil reserves in the Caspian with Russia's Black Sea port of Novorossiisk runs across Chechnya and survived the bloody 21-month conflict with Russia relatively unscathed.
But repairs still need to be made and a compressor near the Azeri border completed.

The Azerbaijan International Operating Company (AIOC), a international consortium of 13 firms, plans to pump over 700,000 barrels of crude per day by 2010 from the Azeri, Chirag and Guneshi fields, partly through the Chechnya pipeline.
It may also pump oil through Georgia via another existing pipeline.
Eventually AIOC will need to build a pipeline for the bulk of its output, which analysts said would probably pass through Georgia to the Turkish port of Ceyhan.

AIOC is headed by the BP/Statoil alliance and includes Azeri state oil firm SOCAR, Amoco Corp, Pennzoil Co, Unocal Corp, Exxon Corp, Ramco Energy Plc, Russia's LUKoil, the Turkish Petroleum Corp, McDermott International Inc, Itochu Corp and Saudia Arabia's Delta Nimir.
Initial reaction to Maskhadov's win was positive among some members of the $8-billion project.
"For us Maskhadov is the best outcome (of the elections)," said a Moscow-based representative of one consortium member.
But Maskhadov still faces major hurdles before he can fulfill his promise to keep oil safe, political analysts said.
He must bring unruly armed factions under his control and stop oil from being siphoned from the pipeline and refined in make-shift factories along the Chechen stretch.
"These are two of the most important tasks," Markov said. "But it seems that he has a good chance of achieving this."
But Maskhadov's victory and apparent willingness to keep oil flowing across Chechnya removes only one of a myriad of political risks faced by companies working in the Caspian.
On Thursday Turkmenistan and Azerbaijan clashed over who owns the oil beneath the Caspian - a spat which some analysts were quick to play down.
"I don't think it will be a serious problem," Markov said.
Moscow also has interests in the region through its national pipeline company Transneft, which says it is in talks with Chechens about transporting oil across the republic.
Russia is smarting from the loss of its Soviet-era control of the Caspian, but its monopoly on oil and gas export pipelines to the West gives it considerable sway over its energy-rich neighbours.
But Zarko Stefanovski, oil analyst at T. Hoare and Co in London, was positive that the states could come to some sort of solution to political problems.
"If Chechnya becomes more stable then we are looking at increased prosperity for the whole region," he said.
